clue.text: Revealed by this fog breaking up? Hardly

definitions.text: Revealed by this fog breaking up? Hardly

parts.note: a secret that has been revealed is out

indicators.note: Fog breaking up is fog coming apart into scattered patches, and letters told to come apart land in a new order.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: Fog thinning over a landscape, and the question of whether it has shown you anything yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: the sentence asks whether the lifting fog has revealed anything and answers its own question, while the same words hand over OUT and seven letters to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue says the thing is hardly revealed even as the fog breaks up, which is what being out of sight amounts to.

clue.text: Master on board climbing wooden mast stops playing

indicators.note: stops in the sense of plugs or fills a gap, so the mast sits inside the other letters
climbing in a down clue means the word reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: oak is a wood, so wooden suggests oak
a spar is a pole such as a mast
V is short for versus, as in one team playing another

explanation.surface: Sailors clamber up a wooden mast and the game stops.
explanation.walkthrough: The ship's mast is a decoy picture: 'on board' means a chessboard, and 'playing' is the versus of a match, not sailors at play.
explanation.definitionFit: Garry Kasparov was world chess champion, a grandmaster at the board.

clue.text: Assumes trouble with Potus regularly

parts.note: much ado about nothing: ado is fuss and trouble

indicators.note: Anything done regularly happens at a fixed interval, so letters are taken at every second position instead of all of them.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters, counted off in twos

explanation.surface: Trouble turning up on schedule wherever the American president goes next.
explanation.walkthrough: POTUS is the standing acronym for the President of the United States, which is what lets the surface read as a news headline instead of a set of letters to count through.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt a name, a pose or a habit is to assume it — both verbs mean taking something on rather than supposing it.

clue.text: I don't like that Republican lout

parts.note: the noise a crowd makes when it does not like what it is watching
R is the standard abbreviation for a Republican in American politics

explanation.surface: A heckler writing off a Republican politician as an oaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I don't like that' is not a synonym but a piece of theatre: the crowd's own noise of disapproval, spelled the way a novel would print it.
explanation.definitionFit: A boor is a coarse, ill-mannered man, which is what 'lout' names, though lout leans more on thuggishness and boor on rudeness.

clue.text: One following gets careless, almost dying

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
next means following

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: remiss means careless or negligent

explanation.surface: The next person in line grows careless and nearly dies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts the final S from REMISS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means at the point of death, used in English for someone in their last moments.

clue.text: Mint tea with a touch of nutmeg added

indicators.note: added in the sense of put into the drink, so these letters go inside the tea

parts.note: a brew is a pot or cup of tea
and means with, in addition to

indicators.note: a touch of something is the smallest amount: its first letter

parts.note: supplies its first letter N

explanation.surface: A recipe for mint tea finished with a grating of nutmeg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' looks like the herb in the tea, but it is the definition, in the sense of mint condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Mint as an adjective means in pristine condition, as new as when it was made.

clue.text: 'Animals' in Post Office beginning to sweat

parts.note: what is in is what is hip — fashionable

indicators.note: A word only beginning is a word not finished, so nothing but its opening letter is taken.

parts.note: PO is the abbreviation on every British high street
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Animals loose in the post office, and somebody starting to perspire about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks flag the first word as a definition by example rather than a synonym, and 'in' is the first piece of wordplay, not the preposition the sentence appears to need.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is one kind of animal among thousands, so the definition works only by example — which is what the quotation marks are owning up to.

clue.text: Sense it could be largely pointless

indicators.note: Largely means for the most part and not the whole of it, so the phrase gives up its final letter.

parts.note: something pointless is no use, written as two words run together

explanation.surface: Somebody dismissing a thing as having no point to it whatever.
explanation.walkthrough: Nous came into English from the Greek for mind and means practical common sense. The wordplay only opens once 'pointless' is read as the phrase 'no use' rather than as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is the down-to-earth kind of sense — gumption, knowing what to do — so 'sense' names it in its everyday British use.

clue.text: Not on the level? Dunno, Paw tricked over 500

indicators.note: Someone tricked has been turned about by another hand, and these letters likewise end up in an arrangement nobody put them in.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, taken as they stand
the Roman numeral for five hundred, joined to the fodder

explanation.surface: A boy mumbling 'dunno' at his father, who has just been swindled out of five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: 'not on the level' reads as dishonest in the surface, which is the sense the swindle sets up, and it means literally not flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up-and-down is not level, and the phrase carries the further sense of erratic — the reading the crooked surface is nudging you towards.

clue.text: Neighbour of 7 right at home wearing nothing

parts.note: R is right, as on a map or in a stage direction
H marks the home team in a printed fixture list
whatever everyone is wearing this season is what is in
the letter shaped like a zero stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A neighbour answering his front door with no clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' looks like a container instruction telling you to slot one piece inside another, and it is a plain synonym here — four small pieces laid end to end, nothing nested.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal at 7 down shares the African plains and the zoo enclosure next door with this one, so the cross-reference defines by neighbourhood rather than by meaning.

clue.text: How many like to solve crosswords in theory?

definitions.text: How many like to solve crosswords
definitions.meaning: with a pen and the printed grid, rather than on a screen
how a plan looks before anybody tries to carry it out

explanation.surface: A survey question about how crossword solvers prefer to tackle the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The join between the two definitions is invisible because 'in theory' finishes the question so naturally that it reads as part of it rather than as a second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Solvers work on paper rather than on a screen, and a scheme that works on paper is one that works in theory but may not survive contact with reality.

clue.text: When reviewing, I used to love her work about new frog genus

indicators.note: about here means next to or around the work, the new letter standing just in front of it
reviewing read as re-viewing, looking back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a former partner is an ex
opus is Latin for a work, especially a musical one

explanation.surface: A man looks back on a former love's work concerning a new kind of frog.
explanation.walkthrough: Xenopus, the African clawed frog, is the genus widely used in laboratories; the frog is the definition, not part of the reminiscence.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenopus is the scientific genus name of the African clawed frogs, widely used in biological research.

clue.text: They're not free to work

definitions.meaning: The surface pushes 'free' towards costing nothing: labour somebody would have to be paid for, rather than labour anyone is at liberty to withhold.
The setter's sense. These are people with no say over whether they work, for whom, or on whose land — the freedom in question is legal, not financial.

explanation.surface: Workers who will not do the job for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to unpick: the whole clue is one description, and the solve is spotting that 'free' means at liberty rather than unpaid, so the sentence is describing a legal status.
explanation.definitionFit: Serfs were bound to a lord's land and could not leave it or hire themselves out elsewhere, so they were literally not free to work where they chose.

clue.text: Breeding grebes in a N Pacific location

indicators.note: Breeding throws two sets of characteristics together into a new one, so what comes out of it is made of the same material in a different combination.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: Grebes nesting somewhere on a stretch of cold northern water.
explanation.walkthrough: Water birds and a sea belong to the same picture, and that is what hides the anagram: 'breeding grebes' reads as a description of the place rather than an instruction about its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bering Sea lies between Siberia and Alaska at the northern limit of the Pacific, so the definition fixes it geographically instead of defining a word.

clue.text: Like Kelvin and the others in bed, not a reliable type

indicators.note: In is the plainest container instruction there is: everything named before it goes inside the word that follows.

parts.note: a bed is the base a thing rests on — a bed of concrete, a bed of gravel
as does the same job as like in a comparison
K is the kelvin, the SI unit of temperature
etc is short for et cetera, Latin for and the rest

explanation.surface: Kelvin and his friends tucked up in bed, one of them not to be counted on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like Kelvin' invites you to picture a bloke, and the wordplay wants the temperature unit's symbol instead — the whole sleeping arrangement is decoration around a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A basket case is someone who cannot cope, so 'not a reliable type' names the person; the phrase began as brutal military slang for a maimed soldier.

clue.text: Scrap music hall staple

definitions.meaning: the rag-and-bone trade's name for whatever waste metal is worth collecting
a song from 1911 that every hall in the country could get an audience singing

explanation.surface: Somebody proposing to scrap the act every music hall used to rely on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Any Old Iron' was Harry Champion's 1911 music hall song, still sung at British singalongs, and its title was lifted straight from the scrap dealer's street cry.
explanation.definitionFit: The rag-and-bone man's cry meant waste metal for sale, which is the first sense, and the same phrase titles the music hall song that made it famous.

clue.text: Yes, I will get move to Reform … and put the boot in?

indicators.note: To reform a thing is to shape it again, and letters reformed are the same letters given a new shape.

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A defector agreeing to a move to Reform and promising to kick his old party while he is at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' is capitalised so that it reads as the political party, and that capital is the whole misdirection — it is an instruction about letters, not a destination.
explanation.definitionFit: Welly is British for a wellington boot and by extension for force, so giving something some welly and putting the boot in are both kicking hard.

clue.text: Where you may find me contracted not natural

parts.note: a speaker would say you can find me in here

indicators.note: contracted means shortened, as not becomes n't, losing its vowel

parts.note: not, with its O dropped, gives NT

explanation.surface: A cryptic remark: look in here and you'll find me shrunken and unnatural.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not natural' reads as a negation, but 'not' is wordplay: 'contracted' shortens it to n't, which follows IN HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: An inherent quality is built in by nature rather than acquired, so it is natural to the thing.

clue.text: Where do soldiers go? Are they required at the front during occupations?

indicators.note: The front of a word is its opening letter, and the front is also where soldiers serve, which is what makes this instruction so easy to walk past.

parts.note: a line of work is an occupation — and an army holds lines too

indicators.note: Whatever happens during something happens inside it, so these letters are set within the word that follows.

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Questions from somebody planning an army camp: where the men go, and what the front line needs.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and wordplay both end in question marks, so nothing marks the seam between them: the first question is the definition and the second is pure instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Latrines are the trench or camp toilets an army digs for itself, so 'where do soldiers go' is a euphemism standing in as a definition.

clue.text: Moves casually round hotel, speed initially being ineffective

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is taken.

parts.note: to tootle is to travel in an unhurried way, as in tootling down the lane

indicators.note: Going round a thing is going about it on every side, so the word before closes over the letter that comes next.

parts.note: H is hotel in the NATO alphabet
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A leisurely amble around a hotel, with speed nowhere in the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface suggests teeth: the hotel and the speed build a picture of somebody dawdling, and 'being' is joinery holding that picture against the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothless means unable to bite, and so, of a law or a watchdog or a threat, unable to have any effect at all.

clue.text: They have a point, debtors admitting

indicators.note: To admit somebody is to let them in, so the word before opens up and takes the other letter inside it.

parts.note: people who owe are owers, the noun the crossword builds straight off the verb
N for north, one of the four points of the compass

explanation.surface: An argument about money in which the people in debt turn out to be right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They have a point' reads as one phrase conceding an argument, and the definition stops two words in — the point is a compass bearing and belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Owners are the people who have things, so 'they have' defines them by the bare fact of possession, which is all the word claims.

clue.text: Books sweetheart into empty Montreal accommodation

indicators.note: into means going inside, so these letters are put within the city's remaining letters
an empty word loses all its inside letters, leaving its first and last

parts.note: emptied it leaves ML
OT, the Old Testament, is a set of books of the Bible
the heart of sweet is its middle letter E

explanation.surface: A traveller books a place for a sweetheart in a deserted Montreal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is not a verb here but OT, the Old Testament. OT and E go 'into' ML.
explanation.definitionFit: A motel is a roadside hotel, so it provides overnight lodging for motorists.

clue.text: Insect (a different one) is trapped under Tom's foot

indicators.note: Trapped under something is held below it, and below in a down entry means later in the answer.
The foot of a word is its bottom end, which in a down entry is its final letter.

parts.note: the last letter of the name, standing at its foot
a different insect from the one being defined
the word itself, lifted straight into the answer

explanation.surface: An insect caught under Tom's shoe, and not the one you would expect to find there.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside is the fairest thing in the clue: it warns you outright that the second creature is wordplay rather than the answer, a courtesy setters rarely extend.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantis is the insect that waits with its forelegs folded as though praying, so 'insect' is the plain category and does nothing more than name it.

clue.text: Type of sex from Thailand grotesque — runs to join in

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: the setter names the kind of sex and leaves you to supply the noun the adjective belongs in front of.

parts.note: T is Thailand's international vehicle code

indicators.note: Joining in means going in among the others, so the letter it introduces is dropped inside the word already assembled.

parts.note: an antic is a grotesque gesture or caper
R is runs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: A lurid holiday story out of Thailand, with somebody hurrying to get involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'grotesque' look like the end of a description of Thailand, when it is a noun the wordplay needs whole before a cricketer's letter is pushed into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tantric names the slow ritual practice drawn from the Tantras, Hindu and Buddhist scriptures, so 'type of sex' points at a tradition rather than an act.

clue.text: Both gutted he's out? Flipping rubbish!

indicators.note: Flipping a thing turns it over, so what has been gathered is read the other way round — and it doubles as the mild swearword the surface wants.
Gutted means the insides have been taken out, and 'both' says to do it to each of the two words that follow, leaving their outsides.

parts.note: the outer letters, with the middle one taken out
the outer letters again, the same operation on the next word

explanation.surface: Two supporters distraught at a batsman being given out, and somebody insisting it was never a dismissal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' works twice over: it is the surface's slang for bitterly disappointed and the instruction to hollow a word out, and 'both' is what tells you the hollowing happens twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosh is British slang for nonsense, so an exclamation of 'rubbish!' is the same dismissal in a different register.

clue.text: Skirt covering nether regions the French rejected for beachwear

indicators.note: A garment covering something has that thing underneath it, so these letters wrap round the piece that follows.

parts.note: a mini is the short skirt of the sixties

indicators.note: What is rejected is thrown out, so the three letters named just before it are removed from the word they sit in.

parts.note: the ankles are the lowest region of the body
les is one of the French words for the, and it is taken away

explanation.surface: A skirt that covers the lower body, turned down by the French in favour of something for the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: A mankini is the sling swimsuit Borat made famous in 2006, so 'beachwear' is being tactful rather than descriptive — and the French here are two syllables of a body part, not a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The mankini is a men's sling swimsuit, so 'beachwear' gives the broad category and stays deliberately bland, since naming the garment would give the joke away.

clue.text: My best friend's letter to Times?

parts.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
t is time, and a pair of them is times

explanation.surface: A letter to the newspaper, apparently written by the writer's closest friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog is proverbially man's best friend, which is the whole definition, and 'Times' is capitalised to point at the newspaper rather than at multiplication.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutt is a mongrel dog, and the dog is proverbially man's best friend, so the definition works through that proverb rather than any dictionary sense.

clue.text: Wrong about hidden warning

indicators.note: Something hidden is tucked away inside something else, so these two letters sit within the word beside them.

parts.note: a wrong is a sin
re means about, as at the head of a memo

explanation.surface: Some wrongdoing kept quiet, and the warning that ought to come with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' is not the extraction instruction it usually is — nothing is spelled out along the clue's own letters here, it is simply saying that one piece goes inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is the wailing alarm that warns of a raid or an emergency, so 'warning' names what the thing exists to do.

clue.text: Do something about sealing gap over light

indicators.note: sealing means closing in, so the gap sits inside the other phrase

parts.note: to see to something is to deal with it

indicators.note: over signals turning the word over, reading it backwards

parts.note: a rift is a gap or split

explanation.surface: Someone told to deal with a gap by sealing it over with light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light' at the end looks like a material for sealing, but it is the verb, to ignite.
explanation.definitionFit: To light something is to ignite it, which is what the phrase means.
